name: Oromo

population.definition: Self-identified ethnic group 'Oromo' in the 2007 Ethiopian census, as tabulated by an academic (Berhanu Abegaz, 2015) from CSA data. Caveats: his national total (74,385,784) differs from the CSA published total I could not open; the same note argues the census undercounted some groups; mother-tongue count in the same table is 25,123,300. The official CSA table itself was NOT readable, so treat this as an academic tabulation, not the CSA figure. For the share, Milkessa Midega (2015) gives Afaan Oromo as 33.8% of mother tongues in the 2007 census.

source.title: Three Million Amara are Missing: An Analysis based on the 1994 and the 2007 Ethiopian Population Censuses (Table 3)
source.publisher: Research note, author's institution (College of William & Mary per author email domain); hosted on ethiopanorama.com
source.author: Berhanu Abegaz
source.quote: Oromo 17,086,454 25,560,625 (self-identification, 1994 and 2007 columns)

facts.claim: In the 2007 census Afaan Oromo was the largest mother tongue in Ethiopia (33.8%), ahead of Amharic (29.3%); in 1994 Amharic had been largest.

source.title: Ethiopian Federalism: The Politics of Linguistic Pluralism and Language Policy Discourses
source.publisher: Ethiopian Journal of Federal Studies, Vol 2 No 2 (Addis Ababa University)
source.author: Milkessa Midega
source.quote: made Afaan Oromo the largest mother tongue in Ethiopia (33.8%) followed by Amharic (29.3%)

facts.claim: Afaan Oromo is written in the Latin alphabet, while Amharic and Tigrigna use Ge'ez script (regional states chose scripts freely).

source.title: Ethiopian Federalism: The Politics of Linguistic Pluralism and Language Policy Discourses
source.publisher: Ethiopian Journal of Federal Studies, Vol 2 No 2
source.author: Milkessa Midega
source.quote: for the languages such as Afaan Oromo, Somali, Sidama, Afar, Gamo, and many others, the Latin alphabet has been preferred.

facts.claim: Four regional languages including Afaan Oromo were elevated to federal working-language status alongside Amharic (announced late February 2020).

source.title: One to five: Ethiopia gets four new federal working languages
source.publisher: Africanews
source.author: Abdur Rahman Alfa Shaban
source.quote: elevated four regional languages to the status of working federal government languages

facts.claim: Before 2020 the federal working language was Amharic only; the 2015 article describes 'federal monolingualism' with regional language autonomy. Oromia's working language is Afan Oromo.

facts.claim: Oromia is the largest regional state in Ethiopia by population and territory; a 2017 estimate gave more than 40 million inhabitants, including non-Oromo residents (Amhara about 7.2%).

facts.claim: The Oromo are described as living in the highlands alongside Amhara and Tigray; the LoC study (1991 edition) gave them about 40 percent of the population (an older, higher estimate than the 2007 census).

facts.claim: The name 'Galla' was the Amhara name for the Oromo in the LoC study's wording; an academic article (Kumsa 2019) discusses it in the context of dehumanising Abyssinian texts and quotes Bale resistance material objecting to 'filthy Galla'. No readable source states outright that 'many Oromo reject it' in neutral wording.
